keyVerseText: Howbeit he refused to turn aside: wherefore Abner with the hinder end of the spear smote him under the fifth rib, that the spear came out behind him; and he fell down there, and died in the same place: and it came to pass, that as many as came to the place where Asahel fell down and died stood still.
rootMeaning: The Hebrew noun חֹמֶשׁ (chômesh) likely derives from an unused root meaning 'to be stout,' which enriches its primary lexical sense as 'the fifth rib' or 'belly.' This etymology suggests a connection to physical fullness or the core of the body, emphasizing not just a skeletal part but the vital, fleshy area around the abdomen. Thus, the literal or root sense captures both the anatomical and the life-sustaining aspects of this region beyond the simple English gloss of 'fifth rib.'
usageInScripture: The word חֹמֶשׁ appears four times in Scripture, consistently referring to the area around the fifth rib or the abdomen. Translations vary slightly, including 'the fifth,' 'him there under the fifth,' and 'him under the fifth,' but all maintain a focus on this specific bodily location. This consistency reveals that חֹמֶשׁ is used to pinpoint a precise anatomical area, often in the context of injury or death, underscoring its significance in narrative descriptions of physical events.
theologicalSignificance: Understanding חֹמֶשׁ as the 'fifth rib' or 'belly' highlights the biblical attention to the vulnerability and mortality of the human body, reminding believers of the frailty and preciousness of life created by God. The focus on this particular part of the body in Scripture points to the reality of human suffering and the consequences of sin, yet also invites reflection on Christ's incarnation and sacrifice, who bore the fullness of human weakness. This word grounds theological meditation on the humanity of Christ and the bodily nature of redemption, affirming that God engages with us in our physicality.
keyVerseReflection: In 2 Samuel 2:23, the phrase 'smote him under the fifth rib' vividly describes the fatal injury inflicted by Abner, with the spear piercing through the body at this precise location. The use of חֹמֶשׁ here conveys not just a random wound but one that strikes at the vital core of the man, underscoring the severity and finality of the attack. This detail deepens the narrative's impact, showing how the language of the body serves to communicate the reality of death and human vulnerability.
